frase_gancho.texto: A stone head with drooping eyelids and bells on its cheeks.

puente_narrativo.texto: From the monument to the conquests, we move on to an image of the myth of Coatepec, the story the Mexica used to explain the triumph of their god Huitzilopochtli.

guion_corto.texto: In March 1830, workers were building houses for the Convent of la Concepción, in the Historic Center of Mexico City. Then a stone head with drooping eyelids came to light. It was Coyolxauhqui, the Mexica goddess of the Moon and sister of Huitzilopochtli. Her name means “she of the bells on her cheeks,” and the sculptor carved it into her face. She wears bell-shaped circles and her lips curve downward, in a gesture of death. According to the myth of Coatepec, Huitzilopochtli beheaded her and hurled her body down the hill. The most curious part is at the bottom, where the neck ends. There, out of sight, the sculptor engraved the sign of water and fire, along with serpents. The abbess of the convent preferred to donate it to the National Museum rather than sell it to foreign collectors.

guion_largo.texto:
A head made of diorite, a greenish stone, is all that remains of Coyolxauhqui in this Mexica sculpture from the Late Postclassic. It came to light in March 1830. Workers were building houses for the Convent of la Concepción, in what is today the Historic Center of Mexico City.

In Mexica tradition, Coyolxauhqui is the goddess of the Moon and the sister of Huitzilopochtli. Her name is explained as “she of the bells on her cheeks.” That is exactly what the artist carved: bell-shaped circles on each cheek. The eyelids fall heavily and the lips curve downward. It is the face of death, worked with enormous delicacy. On her head she wears a cloth headdress with feathers.

The scene it recalls is the myth of Coatepec. Coyolxauhqui and her brothers, the Centzonhuitznahua, wanted to kill their mother, Coatlicue. Then Huitzilopochtli was born, armed with the fire serpent Xiuhcóatl. He defeated his sister, beheaded her and hurled her body down the hill. This head shows the moment of her defeat.

There is a detail that almost no one sees. On the underside, where the severed neck ends, the artist engraved the sign of water and fire, a symbol of sacred war. Serpents accompany it. Those reliefs were out of sight.

The head came close to leaving the country. It is said that foreign diplomats and collectors offered money for it in the nineteenth century. But the abbess of the convent preferred to donate it to the National Museum, and that is how we preserve it today.

texto: Look for the bell-shaped circles on each cheek.
Compare the drooping eyelids with the downward-curving lips.
Notice the cloth headdress with feathers on top of the head.

texto.Origin: Historic Center, Mexico City (Convent of la Concepción)
texto.Dimensions: 72.5 cm high x 85.5 cm wide x 64.5 cm thick

texto.pregunta: Myth: Coyolxauhqui was a warrior queen who really existed.
texto.respuesta: Reality: In Mexica myth she is the goddess of the Moon and the sister of Huitzilopochtli. She is not a historical person.
